content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidance on the regulations for the transport of infectious substances for the years 2017–2018. This document outlines the requirements for the safe and compliant transportation of infectious materials, ensuring the integrity of the substances and the safety of those involved in their handling and transport. The guidelines emphasize the importance of proper packaging, labeling, and documentation to minimize risks during transportation. Under the terms of the WHO license, the document may be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The original English version remains the binding and authentic edition. The document highlights the critical role of shippers in ensuring that packaging and shipping conditions meet regulatory requirements to preserve the integrity of infectious materials and facilitate their timely arrival at their destination. It also addresses the concerns of transport personnel, such as postal workers and airline staff, regarding potential exposure to infectious microorganisms from improperly packaged materials. To mitigate these risks, the packaging must be designed to minimize the potential for damage during transport and ensure the safe handling of specimens. The guidelines provide detailed instructions for classifying infectious substances for transportation and ensuring their safe packaging. They stress the importance of collaboration between senders, carriers, and receivers to ensure the safe and efficient transport of these materials. The document also provides practical guidance to help shippers comply with international regulations for the transport of infectious substances and patient specimens by all modes of transport, both nationally and internationally. Infectious substances are defined as materials known or reasonably expected to contain pathogens, which are microorganisms (e.g., bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) or other agents (e.g., prions) capable of causing disease in humans or animals. The document categorizes infectious substances into two main categories: Category A and Category B. Category A includes substances that, when exposure occurs, can cause permanent disability, life-threatening, or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals. Category B includes substances that do not meet the criteria for Category A but still require careful handling and packaging. The document also addresses the transport of patient specimens, which are human or animal materials collected for purposes such as research, diagnosis, or treatment. These specimens must be packaged and transported in a manner that protects transport personnel from the risk of infection. Additionally, the guidelines cover the transport of biological products, genetically modified microorganisms (GMMOs) and organisms (GMOs), and medical or clinical wastes, providing specific instructions for their classification and handling. The international regulations for the transport of infectious substances are based on recommendations made by the United Nations Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (UNCETDG). These recommendations are presented as Model Regulations and are reflected in international agreements and national legislation. For example, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) publishes legally binding Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air, which are incorporated into the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Dangerous Goods Regulations. Similarly, regulations for road, rail, sea, and postal transport are based on international agreements and conventions. The WHO serves in an advisory capacity to UNCETDG and ICAO, ensuring that its guidelines align with international standards. Many countries adopt the United Nations Model Regulations as their national legislation, while others may apply variations. National authorities are responsible for providing details of their specific requirements. The document also includes definitions and classifications for various terms related to the transport of infectious substances. For example, cultures refer to the intentional propagation of pathogens, while biological products are derived from living organisms and used for prevention, treatment, or diagnosis of diseases. Genetically modified microorganisms and organisms are classified separately and are subject to specific regulations depending on their use and authorization by competent authorities. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide comprehensive instructions for the safe and compliant transport of infectious substances, emphasizing the importance of proper packaging, training, and adherence to international and national regulations. These measures are essential to protect public health, ensure the timely delivery of specimens, and minimize risks to transport personnel.
